title: Elements, Tags, and Attributes
summary: Read HTML as elements made from tags, content, nesting, and attributes, then practice writing balanced markup.

sketchBlocks.title: An HTML element combines tags with its content
sketchBlocks.bodyMarkdown:
An HTML **element** is a meaningful piece of the document represented by markup. Many elements use an opening tag, some content, and a closing tag. The tag name tells the browser what kind of structure the content represents. Reading those three parts together makes HTML much easier to debug. A paragraph element looks like this: ```html

Practice makes markup easier to read.

``` The opening `

` starts the paragraph, the sentence is the content, and `

` closes the paragraph. The slash in the closing tag matters because it tells the browser where that element ends. Some elements, such as `meta`, do not wrap visible text and therefore do not use the same opening-content-closing pattern. You will learn those exceptions as you meet them. For now, build the habit of matching the tags for elements that do wrap content and keeping the intended text between them.

sketchBlocks.title: Nesting shows which content belongs together
sketchBlocks.bodyMarkdown:
HTML **nesting** means placing one element inside another so the document structure shows a parent-and-child relationship. Correct nesting keeps the markup understandable and prevents closing tags from crossing over one another. The inner element should finish before the outer element closes. Here is a worked example: ```html

I am learning semantic HTML today.

``` Read it **line by line** as one nested structure: the paragraph begins first, the `strong` element begins and ends inside that paragraph, and then the paragraph closes. The words “semantic HTML” remain part of the paragraph while receiving stronger importance from the nested element. When markup becomes larger, indentation can make nesting easier to see. The browser may recover from some mistakes, but you should not depend on recovery. Balanced, properly nested elements make the source easier to reason about and give later accessibility and styling work a stronger foundation.

sketchBlocks.title: Attributes add extra information to an element
sketchBlocks.bodyMarkdown:
An HTML **attribute** adds information to an element from inside its opening tag. Attributes usually have a name and a value, and the value is commonly written in quotes. You have already seen useful examples: `lang="en"` describes the document language and `charset="UTF-8"` describes the character encoding. Another simple example is a title attribute on a paragraph: ```html

Welcome to my page.

``` Step by step, `p` is still the element name, `title` is the attribute name, and the quoted text is the attribute value. The visible paragraph content stays between the opening and closing tags. Attributes belong in the opening tag, not between the element's visible words. Different elements support different useful attributes, and later lessons will introduce attributes such as `href`, `src`, and `alt` when you build links and images. For now, practice recognizing the pattern `name="value"` and keeping attributes attached to the element they describe.

quizDraft.title: Recognize a closing tag
quizDraft.prompt: Which option is a closing paragraph tag?
quizDraft.hint: Look for the marker that indicates the element is ending rather than beginning.

help.concept: Paired HTML elements use a closing tag to mark the end of the content they wrap.
help.hint_1: Compare the punctuation immediately after the opening angle bracket.
help.hint_2: The closing form keeps the same element name while adding the end marker.

quizDraft.title: Place an attribute
quizDraft.prompt: Where is an attribute such as lang="en" written?
quizDraft.hint: Think about the part of an element that identifies the tag and its extra information.

help.concept: Attributes describe an element from its opening markup rather than becoming ordinary content text.
help.hint_1: The attribute travels with the element's start tag.
help.hint_2: Do not place attribute syntax after the closing tag or as unrelated body text.

quizDraft.title: Identify element parts
quizDraft.prompt: For a typical paragraph element, which parts can be present?
quizDraft.hint: Compare each choice with the markup example and select only the choices that are actually present in it.

help.concept: Use the exact syntax shown in the example as your evidence. Do not choose an item just because it is related to web pages.
help.hint_1: Check the choices one by one against the example.
help.hint_2: Select every matching choice and leave unrelated choices unselected.

quizDraft.title: Order nested markup
quizDraft.prompt: Arrange these pieces to make a paragraph containing a strong element with valid nesting.
quizDraft.hint: The outer element opens first and closes last.

help.concept: Proper nesting finishes the inner element before the outer element ends.
help.hint_1: Use the parent-child relationship from the worked example.
help.hint_2: The paragraph surrounds the stronger text element rather than crossing its closing tag.

quizDraft.title: Complete the attribute pattern
quizDraft.prompt: Choose the part of an attribute that comes before the equals sign in this example.
quizDraft.hint: Look at the left side of the name-and-value pair.

help.concept: An attribute is written as a name paired with a value inside an opening tag.
help.hint_1: The requested piece labels what information the attribute represents.
help.hint_2: Do not choose the quoted value itself.

quizDraft.title: Name the text between tags
quizDraft.prompt: Choose the term for the text or nested markup between an element's opening and closing tags.
quizDraft.hint: Think about what the tags wrap.

help.concept: A paired element surrounds the material it represents between its start and end markup.
help.hint_1: The requested term describes what belongs inside the element.
help.hint_2: It can be plain text or other properly nested elements.

quizDraft.title: Close the paragraph
quizDraft.prompt: Fix the paragraph so the sentence **Balanced tags are easier to read.** is inside matching opening and closing p tags.
quizDraft.hint: The opening tag is already present; add the matching end tag after the sentence.

help.concept: Balanced paired elements clearly mark where content begins and ends in the document structure.
help.hint_1: Keep the sentence inside the paragraph rather than placing the closing markup before it.
help.hint_2: Compare the element name in the opening tag with the element name in your closing tag.

quizDraft.solutionCode: Balanced tags are easier to read.

quizDraft.title: Nest important text
quizDraft.prompt: Inside the existing paragraph, wrap only the words **HTML structure** in a strong element. Keep the full sentence inside the paragraph.
quizDraft.hint: Place the strong opening and closing tags around the two target words without closing the paragraph early.

help.concept: Nested elements let one part of an outer element carry additional meaning while remaining inside that content.
help.hint_1: The paragraph should open first and close last.
help.hint_2: Check that the strong element begins and ends entirely between the paragraph tags.

quizDraft.solutionCode: I am practicing HTML structure today.

quizDraft.title: Add an attribute
quizDraft.prompt: Add a title attribute with the value **A short introduction** to the paragraph that says **Welcome to my page.** Keep the paragraph text unchanged.
quizDraft.hint: Put the name-and-value pair inside the paragraph's opening tag.

help.concept: An attribute adds information to an element while the element's visible content remains between its tags.
help.hint_1: Keep the quoted value attached to the attribute name with an equals sign.
help.hint_2: Inspect the opening p tag carefully; the visible sentence should stay outside the attribute quotes.
